Accomplice

uh-KOM-plis -- stress on the second syllable, KOM. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Accomplice is a person who helps another commit a crime.

The getaway driver was charged as an accomplice even though he never set foot inside the bank.

Worked Example

While one man distracts the jeweler with questions, his partner quietly slips three watches into a coat pocket; the first man knew the plan all along.

The distracter is an accomplice -- he did not take the watches himself, but he knowingly helped the crime happen. An accomplice is anyone who assists another person in committing a crime.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

abettor: An abettor urges a crime on -- shouting encouragement, goading the offender, cheering the plan forward before or while it happens. An accomplice goes beyond words: an accomplice knowingly helps make the crime happen. Every abettor backs the wrongdoing; an accomplice takes an active hand in it.

confederate: A confederate is a fellow member of the plot -- one of the group that planned the scheme together from the start. Accomplice is the broader legal word: any knowing helper counts as an accomplice, even one recruited at the last minute who never sat in on the planning.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bystander: a person who is present but takes no part

adversary: a person who opposes or works against another

Where it sits · how deeply involved in the wrongdoing — accessory → accomplice → collaborator

accessory vs. accomplice: Accessory is often the lighter legal label -- an accessory may only help at the edges, even after the crime is over, while an accomplice knowingly takes part in making the crime happen.

collaborator vs. accomplice: Collaborator can carry even heavier weight than accomplice: an accomplice helps with a particular crime, while a collaborator -- in its darkest sense -- works hand in hand with an enemy or corrupt power over a sustained period.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ac- (ad-)

prefix — ac- (ad-): to, toward (Latin)

prefix — com-

prefix — com-: together, with (Latin)

root — plice

root — plice: to fold (Latin plicare)

Put it together

Put it together: Accomplice builds on Latin com- ('together') plus plicare ('to fold') -- the same folding found in 'complicity.' An accomplice is literally someone 'folded together with' another: their part in the crime is folded into the criminal's own.

Use the root in a new word: complicated

Use the root in a new word: complicated: The instructions were so complicated that it took three of us to assemble the bookshelf.

Root Check

Word Choice

Accomplice is a legal and journalistic word: an accomplice to a robbery, an accomplice in the scheme. It always implies knowing help with wrongdoing -- someone tricked into helping without understanding the plan is not an accomplice.
